payload.throughline: Follow material, secretions, and signals by asking where each process occurs, what moves or transforms the contents, and what reaches blood, lymph, or the exterior.

learner_content_blocks: Starting check: choose the route that keeps the alimentary compartments in anatomical order. This is low stakes; the full route is taught next.
Purpose: by the end of this cycle, you will be able to locate a digestive event and predict what changes when a compartment, secretion, or movement is disrupted.

The mouth fragments food and mixes it with saliva. The esophagus uses peristaltic waves to propel the bolus. The stomach stores and churns its contents; acid supports protein digestion, while a mucus-and-bicarbonate barrier limits acid injury to the stomach wall.

The small intestine receives neutralizing bicarbonate, bile, and digestive enzymes, completes most chemical digestion, and absorbs most nutrients. The large intestine recovers additional water and houses microbial flora. The rectum stores fecal material before elimination.
Mental model — route, local job, mechanism: first locate the material, then classify the event as movement, secretion, digestion, protection, absorption, or elimination.

Think aloud: a sample is acidic, mixed by muscular contractions, and contains active protein-digesting enzyme. I select the stomach because all three clues converge there; the esophagus transports but does not create that acidic digestive compartment.

Worked trace: after swallowing, peristalsis moves a bolus through the esophagus. The stomach stores, acidifies, and churns it. In the small intestine, acid is neutralized and digestion continues before nutrients cross the epithelium. Remaining material enters the large intestine for water recovery and then the rectum for storage before elimination.
Selection check: do not treat every muscular event as digestion. Peristalsis primarily changes location; churning also mixes contents with secretions.
Guided practice: use the supplied pH, movement, and enzyme clues to identify one compartment. Attend to the combination of clues rather than one familiar word.
Less help: identify the protective mechanism that lets a strongly acidic stomach lumen coexist with living epithelial tissue.
On your own: distinguish propulsion by peristalsis from chemical digestion by a secretion.

Boundary: a secretion can change chemical conditions without moving contents, while a muscular contraction can move or mix contents without cleaving a nutrient. Location alone does not make those functions interchangeable.
Near exit: identify a fresh compartment from its position in the route and its combined processing roles.
Changed-task exit: reason from a selective motility perturbation to the first digestive process expected to decline while secretions remain intact.
Repair the route-function match: locate the clue on the mouth-to-rectum route, then require every stated function to fit the same compartment.
Fresh re-entry: match a different downstream storage-and-elimination clue to the correct compartment. No prior item or answer is reused.
Repair the perturbation function: hold secretions constant, remove only the named muscular movement, and predict the consequence that follows directly from lost movement.
Fresh re-entry: apply that same selective-perturbation reasoning to a different compartment and a different movement.
Recap from memory: say the route in order, then name one movement, one secretion or condition, one protective feature, one absorption site, and the final storage site.
Each failed exit function receives one targeted cue and one fresh re-entry. If that fresh check remains unresolved, control returns for later support without awarding exit success.
Starting check: separate the organ that makes bile from the organ that stores and concentrates it. The complete accessory-organ map follows.
Purpose: you will be able to trace an accessory-organ product to the gut or blood and predict which function changes when one route is selectively disrupted.

The liver lies mainly in the upper right abdomen. It produces bile, processes absorbed nutrients, stores and releases fuel such as glycogen, and transforms many compounds during detoxification. The gallbladder beneath the liver stores and concentrates bile and releases it toward the small intestine.

Bile disperses large lipid droplets into smaller droplets; it is not a bond-cleaving digestive enzyme. The exocrine pancreas sends bicarbonate and digestive enzymes through ducts to the small intestine. Endocrine pancreatic cells release hormones such as insulin and glucagon into blood to regulate blood glucose.
Mental model — product, route, target: liver-made bile and pancreatic digestive secretions travel through ducts to the intestine; pancreatic hormones travel through blood to distant target tissues.

Think aloud: a pancreatic product appears in a duct and acts in the intestinal lumen, so I classify it as exocrine. A pancreatic product measured in blood that changes glucose storage is endocrine; the transport route rules out the alternative.

Worked case: after a fatty meal, the liver has already produced bile. The gallbladder contracts and delivers stored bile to the small intestine, where bile emulsifies lipids. Pancreatic enzymes then gain more accessible lipid-water interface for digestion.
A separate blood-glucose rise recruits endocrine pancreatic signaling, not the pancreatic duct. Keep those two routes distinct even though both begin in the pancreas.
Guided practice: identify the organ that stores liver-made bile before release into the small intestine.
Less help: distinguish physical emulsification by bile from enzymatic hydrolysis of nutrient bonds.
On your own: send a pancreatic product through the correct route—duct to gut or blood to distant targets.

Boundary: bile is produced by liver, stored by gallbladder, and acts in the intestine. Pancreatic enzymes are exocrine; insulin and glucagon are endocrine. Do not assign all four actions to one organ or one transport route.
Near exit: trace bile source, storage, delivery, and immediate action in one coherent chain.
Changed-task exit: use a selective duct obstruction to separate exocrine pancreatic loss from preserved endocrine release.
Repair the bile chain: ask four questions in order—made where, stored where, released where, does what.
Fresh re-entry: reason about bile delivery after loss of storage, using a new situation rather than the original item.
Repair the pancreatic route distinction: duct and intestinal lumen indicate exocrine action; blood and systemic glucose regulation indicate endocrine action.
Fresh re-entry: apply the same route distinction to an endocrine-cell defect while the duct remains open.
Recap from memory: state one liver metabolic role, the bile production-storage-action chain, one pancreatic duct product, and one pancreatic blood-borne function.
The near and changed functions each receive one targeted cue and one untouched re-entry. Persistent uncertainty returns control without converting repair completion into exit success.
Starting check: identify the structural change that increases absorptive area without changing the intestine’s length. Full absorption and control mechanisms follow.
Purpose: you will be able to explain an absorption result from intestinal structure and distinguish a local enteric-control defect from a blood-borne endocrine signaling defect.

Folds, villi, and microvilli enlarge small-intestinal surface area. A thin epithelial barrier places digested nutrients near blood capillaries and lymphatic vessels. Pancreatic enzymes act in the lumen, and brush-border enzymes complete selected reactions at the epithelial surface; bicarbonate helps neutralize gastric acid.

The small intestine absorbs most nutrients and substantial water. The large intestine recovers additional water and supports microbial flora. Enteric neural circuits coordinate local motility and secretion, while digestive hormones travel in blood to targets such as pancreas, gallbladder, stomach, or intestine.

Mental model — surface, route, controller: first identify what crosses the epithelium and by which vascular route; then decide whether the regulating message is a local neural signal or a circulating hormone.

Think aloud: flattened villi reduce surface area while lumen chemistry remains normal. I predict lower nutrient absorption because the exchange interface shrinks; I do not blame pancreatic enzyme production, which the observation preserves.

Worked case: acidic chyme enters the small intestine and is neutralized. Luminal and brush-border enzymes generate absorbable products. Villi and microvilli provide a large epithelial interface, with many water-soluble products entering capillary blood and many packaged lipids entering lymph before reaching blood.
Control check: a local distension-triggered contraction can be coordinated by enteric circuits, whereas a hormone released into blood can alter secretion at a distant digestive target.
Guided practice: use the incoming acidic chyme clue to identify the chemical adjustment needed before many intestinal enzymes work effectively.
Less help: distinguish an enzyme acting in the lumen from one positioned at the brush border.
On your own: connect large-intestinal water recovery and flora to the downstream material that remains after most nutrient absorption.

Boundary: villi increase exchange area but do not themselves secrete every digestive enzyme. Enteric neurons act locally but are not circulating hormones; endocrine signals travel in blood but do not replace all local neural coordination.
Near exit: infer the absorption consequence of a fresh structural change to villi while digestion in the lumen remains intact.
Changed-task exit: use preserved hormone responses and a blocked local neural circuit to isolate the control function that fails first.
Repair the structure-function relation: hold concentration and digestion constant, change only epithelial surface area, and predict the direction of absorption rate.
Fresh re-entry: apply that surface-area relation to a different microscopic structure without reusing the exposed villus item.
Repair the controller distinction: local sensory-motor loops indicate enteric control; a message carried in blood to a named target indicates endocrine control.
Fresh re-entry: apply that distinction to a receptor defect at a hormone target while local enteric circuits remain intact.
Recap from memory: explain one surface-area feature, one neutralization or enzyme site, one water-handling difference, and one contrast between enteric and endocrine control.
Repair is limited to one structure-function cue or one controller-route cue followed by one untouched item. A second miss returns control without claiming the exit was met.
